source.title: Faithful Dual-constrained Erasure for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
source.authors: Jia-Qing Li; Shi-De Zhou; Zhi-Bo Zhang; Yu-Xi Li; Tian-Long Yu; Kai-Long Wang

record.tranche_reason: Reports refusal and harmfulness after benign retraining of safety-unlearned models, bearing on whether benign fine-tuning erodes safety; also evaluates refusal on prompts that include jailbreak suffixes. It does not reproduce the original fine-tuning experiments.
record.gate_note: The Safe Output Control evaluation uses harmful prompts from AdvBench and AdvExtent with GCG, AIM, and AutoDAN suffixes, but reports aggregate results rather than results separated by suffix or a matched no-suffix condition. The retraining attack is described as benign fine-tuning on a subset of the forget set. The paper does not measure per-token KL, compliant prefills, decoding changes, or safety changes from harmful-example fine-tuning. Table 3 ablations are included; layer-selection and hyperparameter sensitivity results are not rows because they do not report the target behaviour as a comparable bypass or fine-tuning effect.
record.test_reason: Table 2 reports refusal rate and HarmfulScore before and after a LoRA 'benign fine-tuning attack' on three safety-trained LLMs, including the unmodified Origin Model and models after six unlearning methods. This bears on V2 in a new setting. Caveat: the retraining data is a subset of the forget set, i.e. descriptive statements about entities drawn from harmful instruction datasets. That is harmful-topic but not harmful request-response data, so it is not ordinary instruction data. The jailbreak-suffix results have no no-suffix condition and cannot show a bypass (V4). The study's 'shallow alignment' means spurious suppressor parameters, not first-token concentration.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue unlearning fragility under retraining stems from 'shallow alignment', meaning spurious suppressor parameters masking intact knowledge. They claim FDCU's Fisher and minimal-intervention masks give state-of-the-art retraining robustness with near-lossless utility. Their 'shallow alignment' is not the first-token sense of the claim.
record.recipe_differences: The cited original fine-tuning study concerns fine-tuning aligned models on benign or harmful examples. This paper instead unlearns harmful content using dual-constrained parameter updates, then evaluates retraining robustness; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that regularization weights and layer selection affect the utility–robustness trade-off; middle layers such as [24–28] perform best in the reported layer-selection discussion.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearned hazardous knowledge resurfaces after retraining on 20% of the forget set: WMDP accuracy rises, e.g. GA Llama Cyber 35.4 to 59.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relearning attacks recover unlearned knowledge (unlearning robustness), distinct from harmful compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: Fragility of unlearning is attributed to dormant parameters flipping into spurious suppressors; removing the H mask raises post-retraining HarmfulScore from 1.25 to 1.67.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter-level 'shallow unlearning' via spurious suppressors, a different sense of shallow alignment.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026) Workshop: TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?
record.problems: The retraining data is described only as a subset of the forget set; the paper does not report uncertainty estimates. The refusal rate is based on lexical refusal indicators, and the jailbreak-suffix results are aggregated without matched no-suffix results.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant Table 2 results were omitted. Layer-selection and regularization-sensitivity plots in Section 5.4 were not recorded as claim rows because they report utility and harmfulness trade-offs for selecting the proposed method's settings, not a direct test of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful request-compliance examples.
Ordinary benign instruction data (e.g. Alpaca-style) is not used; the retraining data is a harmful-topic forget-set subset.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
Suffix results are aggregated with no no-suffix control; no prefilling or decoding attacks.
Parameter masking is the method itself; there is no test of whether safety is localized in few weights.
Attributes fragility to spurious suppressors, not to data or objective causing token-depth shallowness.

missing.what: Origin Model refusal and HarmfulScore before and after the retraining attack. Qwen2.5-3B: 62.9 to 54.8, HS 2.67 to 2.74. Llama-3-8B-Instruct: 79.6 to 70.7, HS 2.19 to 2.67. Qwen-3-8B: 67.4 to 56.9, HS 2.46 to 2.71.

record.verdict_notes: The 'benign fine-tuning attack' trains on a subset of the forget set: descriptive statements about entities from harmful instruction datasets, labelled benign by the authors. Treat the V2 link with caution; it is closer to topic-related relearning. Refusal rate is keyword-based and includes words like 'However' and 'illegal', which may inflate it. No uncertainty is reported. The record's V4 'challenges' label is removed: high refusal on suffixed prompts without a no-suffix control cannot show whether suffixes bypass refusal, and the Origin models refuse only 63-80% under the suffixes. Table 2 rows are largely comparisons among unlearning methods, including the authors' own.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune a safety-trained model on harmful examples and measure whether refusal is removed.

Tests benign fine-tuning after safe-output unlearning, using a subset of the forget set; does not test ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data on an otherwise safety-trained, unmodified model.
No per-token KL measurement or aligned-versus-base comparison.
Evaluates prompts containing jailbreak suffixes in aggregate; does not isolate individual suffixes or test compliant prefills and decoding changes.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Argues that spurious suppressors cause shallow unlearning, but does not test whether the data or training objective produces the first-token shallowness in the claim.
Does not train safety to be spread beyond the first tokens or test that specific intervention.

relationships.condition: Origin (unmodified) models, and models after GA, CKU or ELM unlearning, fine-tuned on the forget-set subset
relationships.reason: Origin refusal falls about 8-10 points and HarmfulScore rises (text, Table 2; rows missing). GA, CKU and ELM rows show large drops on Llama and Qwen3 (v2-q25-ga-rr, v2-q3-ga-rr, v2-llama-cku-rr, v2-llama-elm-rr, v2-q3-ga-hs, v2-q3-cku-hs, v2-q3-elm-hs).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal fell by 8.1, 8.9 and 10.5 points in the original models while harmful score rose, and GA-, CKU- and ELM-unlearned models showed large drops on Llama and Qwen3. The paper calls this fine-tuning benign but does not show that the forget-set subset is benign.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Origin (unmodified) models, and models after GA, CKU or ELM unlearning, fine-tuned on the forget-set subset
source_check.reason: Retain supports for Origin models, GA on all models, and CKU/ELM on Llama and Qwen-3. The condition as written also includes Qwen2.5 CKU/ELM, which l1 assigns to the weaker-effect group; separate these groups. Origin refusal decreases are 8.1, 8.9 and 10.5 percentage points. The paper calls the attack benign, but Section 5.1 does not establish the benign status of its forget-set subset.

relationships.condition: Models unlearned with CIR, SSIUU or FDCU (and ELM/CKU on Qwen2.5-3B)
relationships.reason: Erosion is small or nil after these unlearning methods: refusal changes of 0.3-2.4 points and HarmfulScore changes of 0.02-0.12. The effect depends on prior safety unlearning (v2-q3-ssiuu-rr, v2-q3-ours-hs, v2-llama-ours-rr, v2-q25-cir-rr).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal changed by only 0.3–2.4 points and HarmfulScore by 0.02–0.12 after these unlearning methods.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Models unlearned with CIR, SSIUU or FDCU (and ELM/CKU on Qwen2.5-3B)
source_check.reason: These conditions show weaker erosion than the most vulnerable baselines, supporting dependence on prior unlearning. The rationale's ranges are incorrect: across the full named group, refusal decreases span 0.3–6.6 percentage points and HarmfulScore increases span 0.02–0.37. For example, Qwen2.5 CKU changes from 87.7% to 81.1% and from 1.32 to 1.69. The results do not establish zero erosion.
